title: Adaptive-Group Process Rewards for GUI Agents

paper.title: Adaptive-Group Process Rewards for GUI Agents
paper.abstract:
Abstract Training graphical user interface (GUI) agents with reinforcement learning suffers from sparse outcome rewards, leading to inefficient learning.
Process rewards offer a promising direction for credit assignment to intermediate actions; however, accurately evaluating an action requires identifying evidence across long-horizon GUI trajectories, as its value may depend on information beyond its immediate state and observation.
In this paper, we propose an adaptive-group process reward framework that dynamically partitions a GUI trajectory into semantically coherent subgoal groups, enabling process reward estimation at both the action and group levels.
At the action level, a critic evaluates each action based on the visual changes and subsequent actions within the group for action correctness and contribution to the subgoal.
At the group level, the framework aggregates action-level evaluations to assess subgoal completion and contribution to the overall task, and further refines these assessments by leveraging the context of all groups in the trajectory.
The process reward of each action is obtained by combining its action-level evaluation with the refined group-level evaluation.
We further augment GRPO’s outcome advantage with the proposed process rewards to provide finer-grained guidance for GUI agent training.
Experiments on process reward benchmarks and downstream RL training demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recent advances in large language models and vision-language models have enabled graphical user interface (GUI) agents Cheng et al. (2024) ; Hong et al. (2024) ; Qin et al. (2025) ; Lin et al. (2024) ; Xu et al. (2025) ; Gao et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2025) . These agents translate user instructions and visual observations into executable interactions across digital devices, with applications such as software testing, office assistance, and industrial automation. GUI tasks typically involve long-horizon, multi-turn interactions Zhou et al. (2023) ; Rawles et al. (2024) ; Xie et al. (2025) , requiring agents to maintain multimodal interaction context across changing visual states and coordinate sequences of actions. Reinforcement learning (RL) Li et al. (2025) ; Xiao et al. (2025) ; Lu et al. (2025) ; Tang et al. (2026) is well suited to such interactive tasks, allowing agents to improve their policies based on feedback from the GUI environments. Most GUI environments provide reward signals primarily in the form of sparse outcome rewards Xie et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025) : a trajectory is judged successful if the final application state satisfies the instruction requirement, and unsuccessful otherwise. Consequently, the outcome-level signal is assigned to all intermediate actions in a trajectory, failing to distinguish useful actions from redundant or incorrect ones and making credit assignment unreliable. Process rewards Lightman et al. (2023) ; Wang et al. (2023) ; Chen et al. (2025) are therefore needed to evaluate intermediate actions. However, constructing reliable process rewards for GUI trajectories is challenging because GUI environments rarely provide direct supervision for intermediate actions. Whether an action is correctly executed can often be verified from the current and subsequent observations, whereas whether its semantic purpose is correct may only become clear after subsequent actions. Judging the action requires evidence from a broader trajectory context than the immediate state change after that action alone. Existing GUI process reward methods typically organize trajectory evidence and assign credit through two types of preset context scopes: fixed-window step rewards Chen et al. (2025) ; Xiong et al. (2025) ; Xiao et al. (2025) ; Lu et al. (2025) ; Wan et al. (2026) and milestone rewards Zheng et al. (2026) ; Hao et al. (2026) ; Li et al. (2026a) ; Dai et al. (2026a) ; Zhai et al. (2026) . Fixed-window step rewards evaluate an action within a fixed local context (figure 1 (a)). Short windows may miss long-range evidence needed to assess the action’s effect, whereas longer windows may introduce irrelevant context. Milestone rewards instead predefine task progress around fixed checkpoints or subgoals (figure 1 (b)). Because GUI tasks may admit multiple valid execution paths, such milestones can under-credit progress that does not follow the predefined path and overlook the intermediate actions connecting checkpoints. Thus, an effective process reward should adapt its evidence scope and credit assignment to the executed trajectory, rather than relying on fixed local scopes or predefined checkpoints. Figure 1: Fixed-window step rewards, milestone rewards, and adaptive-group process rewards on an executed GUI trajectory. (a) A fixed local window can include irrelevant context and miss later evidence. (b) Predefined milestones can leave a valid executed path uncredited. (c) Adaptive groups follow the executed subgoals and score actions within each group. In this paper, we introduce an adaptive-group process reward framework for GUI trajectories (figure 1 (c)). Using the task instruction and the agent’s responses, the executed trajectory is dynamically partitioned into consecutive groups of actions that share the same subgoal or semantic operation, rather than by a fixed partition rule. This grouping defines the context for judging the actions in each group and supports two complementary levels of evaluation. At the action level, the critic assesses whether each action is correctly executed based on the local visual change and whether it advances the group’s subgoal based on later actions in the group. At the group level, the critic aggregates the action-level assessments within each group to assess its subgoal completion and contribution to the whole task. Then, the produced group-level assessments are revisited in the context of all groups, allowing the critic to judge each group’s role beyond its local evidence. The process reward of each action is obtained by combining its action-level assessment with the refined group-level assessment of its group. We further use the generated process rewards to shape the GRPO Shao et al. (2024) advantage at each step, providing finer-grained credit assignment during policy optimization. We evaluate the framework on process-reward benchmarks and in downstream RL on OSWorld. The results show consistent improvements in process-reward accuracy and task success rate, demonstrating the effectiveness of adaptive-group process rewards. Our contributions are as follows: • We introduce an adaptive-group process reward framework for GUI agents, which dynamically partitions trajectories into semantically coherent subgoal groups to organize the evidence needed for process reward evaluation. • We design a two-level evaluation that assesses execution and contribution at both the action level and the group level, and obtain the process reward of each action by combining these assessments, making correct execution and group-level contribution jointly necessary. • Experiments on process reward benchmarks and downstream RL training demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

sections.heading: 2.1 GUI Agents
sections.text: Recent progress in large language models and vision-language models has enabled GUI agents that interact with applications through visual observations and executable actions. Early systems mainly relied on prompting or supervised fine-tuning, while recent open-source models and frameworks, such as ShowUI Lin et al. (2024) , CogAgent Hong et al. (2024) , AGUVIS Xu et al. (2025) , UI-TARS Qin et al. (2025) , OpenCUA Wang et al. (2025) , Agent S Agashe et al. (2024) , and TongUI Zhang et al. (2025) , improve grounding, planning, and cross-platform interaction through larger GUI data and stronger vision-language-action modeling. More recently, reinforcement learning has become a central direction for GUI agents because it can optimize long-horizon interaction from environment feedback rather than only imitating fixed demonstrations. DART Li et al. (2025) decouples multi-turn rollout from training for GUI RL, UI-Genie Xiao et al. (2025) builds a reward-guided self-improvement loop for mobile GUI agents, Orcust Lu et al. (2025) combines principle-constrained reward modeling with online VM-grounded trajectory construction, and ClawGUI Tang et al. (2026) provides a full-stack infrastructure for GUI agent RL and deployment. However, most RL pipelines still rely heavily on sparse outcome rewards, which makes it difficult to assign credit to intermediate actions. Our work addresses this limitation by constructing dense process rewards over adaptive groups and the actions in those groups.

sections.heading: 2.2 Process Reward Modeling
sections.text: Process reward modeling supplements sparse outcome rewards with feedback on intermediate steps, enabling more fine-grained credit assignment during training. In reasoning Lightman et al. (2023) ; Wang et al. (2023) and coding Le et al. (2022) ; Liu et al. (2023) ; Dai et al. (2026b) tasks, intermediate feedback can often be verified from execution results, compiler errors, unit tests, or other deterministic checks. GUI tasks provide no comparable automatic signal for most intermediate operations: the value of a click, text entry, menu selection, or file operation depends on visual state changes, task requirements, and subsequent operations. GUI process reward modeling must therefore infer both whether an action is correctly executed and its semantic role from trajectory context. Existing GUI process reward methods can be broadly organized into fixed-window step rewards Chen et al. (2025) ; Xiong et al. (2025) ; Xiao et al. (2025) ; Lu et al. (2025) ; Wan et al. (2026) and milestone rewards Zheng et al. (2026) ; Hao et al. (2026) ; Li et al. (2026a) ; Dai et al. (2026a) ; Zhai et al. (2026) . Fixed-window step rewards judge actions within a fixed local context. GUI-Shepherd Chen et al. (2025) learns step-level scores and rationales from human annotations, while GUI-PRA Xiong et al. (2025) selects historical context and actively perceives UI state changes to improve step-level judgment. SeekJudge Wan et al. (2026) further targets fine-grained step-level judgments for use within reinforcement learning. Milestone rewards organize feedback around predefined subgoals, checkpoints, or broader task-level structures. ADMIRE Zheng et al. (2026) dynamically distills verifiable milestones from successful explorations and applies asymmetric credit assignment to successful and failed trajectories. StainFlow Hao et al. (2026) tracks entity evidence to derive task stages and links relevant steps for key-node verification, while GUIDE Zhai et al. (2026) decomposes completed trajectories into subtask units for structured diagnosis. These approaches organize action judgment within preset local contexts or task-level structures, whereas our adaptive-group framework dynamically partitions the executed trajectory into semantically coherent subgoal groups and combines execution and contribution at both the action level and the group level to assign each action a process reward.

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem Formulation
sections.text: We formulate solving a GUI task as a sequential interaction between an agent and an environment. Given a task instruction g g , the agent observes the GUI state o t o_{t} at each step. Conditioned on this observation and the interaction history, it generates a response c t c_{t} with an executable action a t a_{t} . Executing a t a_{t} changes the environment and produces the next observation o t + 1 o_{t+1} . An executed trajectory is therefore represented as τ = ( o 0 , c 0 , a 0 , o 1 , c 1 , a 1 , … , o T − 1 , c T − 1 , a T − 1 , o T ) , \tau=(o_{0},c_{0},a_{0},o_{1},c_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{T-1},c_{T-1},a_{T-1},o_{T}), (1) where T T is the number of executed actions. The response c t c_{t} provides the agent’s textual intent, while the observations and executed actions record the interaction with GUI. After the trajectory is completed, the environment or a task verifier V V produces an outcome reward R = V ⁡ ( g , τ ) R=V(g,\tau) . This trajectory-level signal does not directly indicate the value of individual actions. We therefore formulate GUI process reward generation as producing a process reward for every executed action: ( r 0 pr , r 1 pr , … , r T − 1 pr ) = ϕ ⁡ ( g , τ ) , (r_{0}^{\mathrm{pr}},r_{1}^{\mathrm{pr}},\ldots,r_{T-1}^{\mathrm{pr}})=\phi(g,\tau), (2) where ϕ \phi is a process reward model and r t pr r_{t}^{\mathrm{pr}} is the process reward of action a t a_{t} at step t t . As shown in figure 2 , we instantiate ϕ \phi by first partitioning τ \tau into adaptive groups that define the context for judging each action (section 3.2 ), then generating action-level and group-level assessments (section 3.3 ). The resulting process rewards are used to shape GRPO’s step-level advantage during policy optimization (section 3.4 ). Figure 2: Overview of the proposed framework. (a) A grouping critic partitions the trajectory from the instruction and responses into subgoal groups. (b) Two-level scoring produces an action-level score and a refined group-level score, which are used to generate the process rewards. (c) The process rewards shape the GRPO advantage.

sections.heading: 3.2 Adaptive-Group Trajectory Partitioning
sections.text: Fixed-window step rewards evaluate an action within a preset local context, while milestone rewards organize credit around predefined checkpoints. Neither evidence scope is determined by the trajectory that was actually executed. We recover subgoals from the executed trajectory instead. Grouping should follow executed intents, which are already stated in each c t c_{t} , so we use a grouping critic F part F_{\mathrm{part}} to partition the trajectory from the instruction g g and the responses { c t } t = 0 T − 1 \{c_{t}\}_{t=0}^{T-1} : { G k } k = 1 K = F part ​ ( g , { c t } t = 0 T − 1 ) , G k = ( n k , ℐ k ) . \{G_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}=F_{\mathrm{part}}(g,\{c_{t}\}_{t=0}^{T-1}),\qquad G_{k}=(n_{k},\mathcal{I}_{k}). (3) The result is a contiguous, non-overlapping partition of the trajectory: each G k G_{k} consists of a hypothesized subgoal n k n_{k} and the step indices ℐ k \mathcal{I}_{k} of the group, and k ⁡ ( t ) k(t) denotes the unique group of step t t . The subgoal n k n_{k} is not a required milestone of g g , so valid executions can induce different groups. These groups are the context for the judgments below.

sections.heading: 3.3 Adaptive-Group Process Reward Generation
sections.text: The adaptive group defines the context for judging its actions and supports two complementary levels of evaluation: how an action contributes to the group’s subgoal, and how the subgoal contributes to the overall task. At the action level, the critic assesses whether each action is correctly executed and whether it advances the group’s subgoal. At the group level, it aggregates these assessments to judge the group’s subgoal completion and contribution to the global task, then revisits the group-level assessments using all groups as context. Verifying execution can be done from the current and next observations, whereas judging semantic purpose depends on what follows: later actions in the group for an action, and other groups for a subgoal. To score an action or a group, the executed actions have to be interpreted against the instruction. We therefore first use a reference critic F ref F_{\mathrm{ref}} to build, for each G k G_{k} , an instruction-conditioned reference u k u_{k} from g g , G k G_{k} , and the group’s responses { c t } t ∈ ℐ k \{c_{t}\}_{t\in\mathcal{I}_{k}} , to inform the two levels of scoring that follow: u k = ( u k tgt , u k cst , u k prc ) = F ref ​ ( g , G k , { c t } t ∈ ℐ k ) . u_{k}=(u_{k}^{\mathrm{tgt}},u_{k}^{\mathrm{cst}},u_{k}^{\mathrm{prc}})=F_{\mathrm{ref}}(g,G_{k},\{c_{t}\}_{t\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}). (4) u k tgt u_{k}^{\mathrm{tgt}} is the target state implied by g g for this group, u k cst u_{k}^{\mathrm{cst}} the checkable constraints, and u k prc u_{k}^{\mathrm{prc}} the preferred process. Action-level scoring consults u k cst u_{k}^{\mathrm{cst}} when checking whether the change from o t o_{t} to o t + 1 o_{t+1} is consistent with the instruction; group-level scoring consults u k tgt u_{k}^{\mathrm{tgt}} and u k prc u_{k}^{\mathrm{prc}} when judging whether the group advances the task and whether the attempted route is reasonable. We treat u k u_{k} as a scoring reference rather than as a strict prior: the trajectory is not required to follow u k prc u_{k}^{\mathrm{prc}} or to attain u k tgt u_{k}^{\mathrm{tgt}} , and an alternative path that still satisfies g g remains valid.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Benchmarks. We evaluate the proposed process rewards on two process-reward benchmarks and for reinforcement learning on OSWorld applications. CUARewardBench Lin et al. (2026) is built on OSWorld trajectories from 10 desktop software categories and 7 agents; it annotates key good and bad actions, and we report process-reward results compared to the benchmark’s OpenCUA-Reflector Wang et al. (2025) and SE-WSM Sun et al. (2025) prompt templates. CUAStepBench Wan et al. (2026) densely annotates every step on executed computer-use trajectories and pairs these labels with human trajectory-level verdicts, covering 177 applications across platforms. OSWorld Xie et al. (2025) provides open-ended GUI tasks in a real desktop environment, with success judged by execution-based scripts on the final state; we train and test on its Chrome, LibreOffice Impress, and LibreOffice Calc applications. Metrics. CUARewardBench treats each step judgment as a binary decision against a human label. We use a threshold of 0.4 0.4 to separate positive and negative predictions. We follow the benchmark protocol: precision (P) and negative predictive value (NPV) measure how reliable a positive or negative verdict is, while recall (R), specificity (S), and overall accuracy (OA) summarize coverage and overall correctness. On CUAStepBench, every step carries a binary human label, and we score the predicted step judgments by precision (P), recall (R), and F1. OSWorld success is determined by execution-based scripts on the final desktop state; we report both a single-run success rate and the mean over three runs. Implementation. We use Qwen3.6-27B Qwen Team (2026) for F part F_{\mathrm{part}} , F ref F_{\mathrm{ref}} , F act F_{\mathrm{act}} , F grp F_{\mathrm{grp}} , and F rev F_{\mathrm{rev}} . We build on the open-source DART-GUI infrastructure Li et al. (2025) for reinforcement learning: multi-turn OSWorld rollouts are collected independently of training, stored, and consumed by an asynchronous GRPO trainer. Our framework for process-reward generation is integrated as an additional asynchronous stage on completed trajectories, and the trainer then uses these process rewards to shape the GRPO advantage of the base model UI-TARS-1.5-7B Qin et al. (2025) . Rollouts use N = 8 N=8 trajectories per instruction, 15 concurrent environments, a maximum of 30 environment steps, and sampling temperature 0.7 0.7 ; each action is generated with at most 5 images and 35 text turns of history. GRPO training uses learning rate 1 × 10 − 7 1\times 10^{-7} , KL coefficient 0.1 0.1 , clip range [ 0.1 , 0.28 ] [0.1,0.28] , and process-advantage coefficient α = 0.5 \alpha=0.5 . Baselines. On CUARewardBench, we compare against the official baselines: general vision-language models (Qwen2.5-VL Bai et al. (2025b) , Qwen3-VL Bai et al. (2025a) , GLM-4.5V V Team et al. (2025) , and GPT-5 OpenAI (2025) ) and GUI models (GUI-Owl Ye et al. (2025) and SE-WSM Sun et al. (2025) ). We also run the same Qwen3.6-27B under the official templates. On CUAStepBench, we compare against CUAJudge Xue et al. (2026) , OSThemis Li et al. (2026b) , and SeekJudge Wan et al. (2026) , including SeekJudge with the same Qwen3.6-27B backbone. sections.heading: 4.2 Process Reward Evaluation
sections.text: Tables 1 and 2 compare the proposed framework with official CUARewardBench baselines run under the OpenCUA-Reflector and SE-WSM prompt templates, respectively. Table 3 reports precision, recall, and F1 for identifying error steps on CUAStepBench. As shown in Tables 1 and 2 , our framework achieves the highest overall accuracy ( 81.3 81.3 ), 3.6 3.6 points above GPT-5 with OpenCUA-Reflector ( 77.7 77.7 ) and 6.4 6.4 points above GPT-5 with SE-WSM ( 74.9 74.9 ). Our framework also improves overall accuracy by 14.0 14.0 points over the same Qwen3.6-27B backbone under OpenCUA-Reflector ( 67.3 67.3 ) and by 10.5 10.5 points under SE-WSM ( 70.8 70.8 ), demonstrating that the gain comes from the grouping and two-level scoring rather than from a stronger judge model. The two official templates also differ: OpenCUA-Reflector gives higher recall but lower specificity, and SE-WSM gives higher specificity but lower recall (e.g., Qwen3.6-27B at 95.1 95.1 / 36.6 36.6 vs. 69.8 69.8 / 72.0 72.0 ; GPT-5 at 92.3 92.3 / 61.6 61.6 vs. 64.8 64.8 / 86.0 86.0 ), while our framework keeps a more even trade-off ( 87.8 87.8 recall, 73.9 73.9 specificity). We then evaluate our framework on CUAStepBench, as shown in Table 3 . Our framework achieves the highest F1 ( 39.9 39.9 ), 1.8 1.8 points above SeekJudge-9B ( 38.1 38.1 ). With the same Qwen3.6-27B backbone, SeekJudge reaches only 36.3 36.3 F1, while our framework improves F1 by 3.6 3.6 points. Our framework also achieves the highest recall ( 57.2 57.2 ), at lower precision ( 30.6 30.6 vs. 44.0 44.0 ), thus missing fewer error steps.

sections.text: As shown in Table 5 , we ablate grouping on CUARewardBench. Ours uses adaptive grouping from the instruction and the agent’s responses. Single-group places all actions in one group. Fixed-window denotes the fixed-window step-reward methods described in section 1 , using consecutive windows of 5 screenshots. Grouping w/ screenshots uses screenshots as extra input when partitioning. Ours achieves the highest overall accuracy ( 81.3 81.3 ). Single-group lowers overall accuracy to 75.7 75.7 , which shows that splitting the trajectory into subgoal groups is useful because a subgoal is specific enough to tell useful actions from redundant or incorrect ones, rather than judging them against the whole task. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we present an adaptive-group process reward framework that dynamically partitions a GUI trajectory into semantically coherent subgoal groups, enabling process reward estimation at both the action and group levels. The process reward of each action is obtained by combining its action-level evaluation with the refined group-level evaluation. These process rewards are used to shape GRPO’s step-level advantage during policy optimization. Experiments on process reward benchmarks and downstream RL training demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

sections.text: As shown in Table 8 , we compare sampling throughput during OSWorld RL with and without our framework, under synchronous and asynchronous scoring. sections.heading: C.1 Error Analysis
sections.text: We analyze 63 63 critic error steps on CUARewardBench, which fall into four categories (Table 9 ). Insufficient application knowledge ( 41.3 % 41.3\% ) is the largest share: the critic does not know the correct menu, setting, syntax, or operator, so its reference treats a wrong path as the intended procedure (e.g., Password Manager instead of cookie settings, Insert-Comment instead of View-Notes, or a Calc sheet reference written with “!” rather than “.”). Visual or interaction misreads ( 22.2 % 22.2\% ) are screenshot-level mistakes: a later date read as earlier, a filter chip taken as on, a slider taken as max, or a click that did not register. Missed instruction constraints ( 19.0 % 19.0\% ) are cases where g g already specifies the requirement—working directory, numeric target, time range, “on sale”—but the critic scores the step without enforcing it. Overestimated group contribution ( 17.5 % 17.5\% ): the group-level score still treats a subgoal as helping the task when it does not (e.g., a group that resizes one layer when the task is to resize the whole image). sections.text: Figures 3 , 4 , and 5 visualize the adaptive-group process rewards on three CUARewardBench trajectories. Each cell shows the screenshot, the action, and the action-level score. A colored box groups consecutive steps of the same subgoal and shows the refined group-level score and contribution. Figure 3: A Chrome trajectory for enabling Do Not Track. Figure 3 never turns on Do Not Track, but Groups 1–2 (“Navigate to Chrome Settings” and “Navigate to Privacy and Security Section”) still score opening Settings and Privacy and security as useful, instead of giving every step a zero because the trajectory fails. In Group 3, clicking “Site settings” is exploratory and the back arrow is Useful-efficient (it undoes the wrong page); Group 4 scores “Privacy guide” the same way, then lowers that group to redundant because Group 3 has already shown the setting is not there. Group 5 scores going back to “Site settings” as useful, but the premature DONE as 0 0 . Figure 4: A Calc trajectory that fills the Seq No. column with “No. #”. Figure 4 fills the column only after Group 2 (“Attempt to auto-fill sequence (First Attempt)”) fails. If only the final outcome were used, the misclick that opens Activities would get the same success credit as the later fill. Grouping puts typing “No. 1” and “No. 2” in Group 1 (“Enter initial sequence values”), the failed fill in Group 2, and the retry in Group 3 (“Retry auto-fill sequence (Second Attempt)”), so the successful retry does not change the scores of the failed attempt. In Group 2, the click that opens Activities and the missed fill handle are harmful, Esc is Useful-efficient (it closes Activities and returns to Calc), and the group stays exploratory because the column is still empty; Group 3 then scores the same fill as useful after “No. #” appears. Figure 5: A failure-case trajectory that opens the first link in the latest Bills email in a new Chrome tab. The dashed outline marks the incorrectly scored step. Figure 5 shows a failure case: the process reward is wrong at the dashed step. The instruction asks for the latest email in the Bills folder. The list shows an AWS invoice dated 3 / 1 / 2024 3/1/2024 above an X receipt dated 12 / 1 / 2024 12/1/2024 ; 12 / 1 / 2024 12/1/2024 is later, so the second mail should be opened. The critic compares the two dates incorrectly, treats 3 / 1 / 2024 3/1/2024 as newer, and scores clicking the AWS invoice as 1.0 1.0 . This is a visual-judgment error limited by the capability of the model used as the critic: it is not reliable enough at reading a small UI detail such as which of two dates is later.

Affiliation: BIGAI Affiliation: BIGAI, Wuhan University Affiliation: BIGAI, Shenzhen MSU-BIT University Affiliation: BIGAI Xinxiao Wu † † thanks: Corresponding author. wuxinxiao@bit.edu.cn Affiliation: Beijing Key Laboratory of Intelligent Information Technology, School of Computer Science & Technology, Beijing Institute of Technology; Affiliation: Guangdong Laboratory of Machine Perception and Intelligent Computing, Shenzhen MSU-BIT University. Affiliation: BIT, BIGAI Affiliation: BIT, Shenzhen MSU-BIT University Lifeng Fan Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of General Artificial Intelligence, BIGAI; Affiliation: BIGAI Affiliation: BIGAI, Wuhan University Affiliation: BIGAI, Shenzhen MSU-BIT University Affiliation: BIGAI Abstract Training graphical user interface (GUI) agents with reinforcement learning suffers from sparse outcome rewards, leading to inefficient learning. Process rewards offer a promising direction for credit assignment to intermediate actions; however, accurately evaluating an action requires identifying evidence across long-horizon GUI trajectories, as its value may depend on information beyond its immediate state and observation. In this paper, we propose an adaptive-group process reward framework that dynamically partitions a GUI trajectory into semantically coherent subgoal groups, enabling process reward estimation at both the action and group levels. At the action level, a critic evaluates each action based on the visual changes and subsequent actions within the group for action correctness and contribution to the subgoal. At the group level, the framework aggregates action-level evaluations to assess subgoal completion and contribution to the overall task, and further refines these assessments by leveraging the context of all groups in the trajectory. The process reward of each action is obtained by combining its action-level evaluation with the refined group-level evaluation. We further augment GRPO’s outcome advantage with the proposed process rewards to provide finer-grained guidance for GUI agent training. Experiments on process reward benchmarks and downstream RL training demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. 1 Introduction Recent advances in large language models and vision-language models have enabled graphical user interface (GUI) agents Cheng et al. (2024) ; Hong et al. (2024) ; Qin et al. (2025) ; Lin et al. (2024) ; Xu et al. (2025) ; Gao et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2025) . These agents translate user instructions and visual observations into executable interactions across digital devices, with applications such as software testing, office assistance, and industrial automation. GUI tasks typically involve long-horizon, multi-turn interactions Zhou et al. (2023) ; Rawles et al. (2024) ; Xie et al. (2025) , requiring agents to maintain multimodal interaction context across changing visual states and coordinate sequences of actions. Reinforcement learning (RL) Li et al. (2025) ; Xiao et al. (2025) ; Lu et al. (2025) ; Tang et al. (2026) is well suited to such interactive tasks, allowing agents to improve their policies based on feedback from the GUI environments. Most GUI environments provide reward signals primarily in the form of sparse outcome rewards Xie et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025) : a trajectory is judged successful if the final application state satisfies the instruction requirement, and unsuccessful otherwise. Consequently, the outcome-level signal is assigned to all intermediate actions in a trajectory, failing to distinguish useful actions from redundant or incorrect ones and making credit assignment unreliable. Process rewards Lightman et al. (2023) ; Wang et al. (2023) ; Chen et al. (2025) are therefore needed to evaluate intermediate actions. However, constructing reliable process rewards for GUI trajectories is challenging because GUI environments rarely provide direct supervision for intermediate actions. Whether an action is correctly executed can often be verified from the current and subsequent observations, whereas whether its semantic purpose is correct may only become clear after subsequent actions. Judging the action requires evidence from a broader trajectory context than the immediate state change after that action alone. Existing GUI process reward methods typically organize trajectory evidence and assign credit through two types of preset context scopes: fixed-window step rewards Chen et al. (2025) ; Xiong et al. (2025) ; Xiao et al. (2025) ; Lu et al. (2025) ; Wan et al. (2026) and milestone rewards Zheng et al. (2026) ; Hao et al. (2026) ; Li et al. (2026a) ; Dai et al. (2026a) ; Zhai et al. (2026) . Fixed-window step rewards evaluate an action within a fixed local context (figure 1 (a)). Short windows may miss long-range evidence needed to assess the action’s effect, whereas longer windows may introduce irrelevant context. Milestone rewards instead predefine task progress around fixed checkpoints or subgoals (figure 1 (b)). Because GUI tasks may admit multiple valid execution paths, such milestones can under-credit progress that does not follow the predefined path and overlook the intermediate actions connecting checkpoints. Thus, an effective process reward should adapt its evidence scope and credit assignment to the executed trajectory, rather than relying on fixed local scopes or predefined checkpoints. Figure 1: Fixed-window step rewards, milestone rewards, and adaptive-group process rewards on an executed GUI trajectory. (a) A fixed local window can include irrelevant context and miss later evidence. (b) Predefined milestones can leave a valid executed path uncredited. (c) Adaptive groups follow the executed subgoals and score actions within each group. In this paper, we introduce an adaptive-group process reward framework for GUI trajectories (figure 1 (c)). Using the task instruction and the agent’s responses, the executed trajectory is dynamically partitioned into consecutive groups of actions that share the same subgoal or semantic operation, rather than by a fixed partition rule. This grouping defines the context for judging the actions in each group and supports two complementary levels of evaluation. At the action level, the critic assesses whether each action is correctly executed based on the local visual change and whether it advances the group’s subgoal based on later actions in the group. At the group level, the critic aggregates the action-level assessments within each group to assess its subgoal completion and contribution to the whole task. Then, the produced group-level assessments are revisited in the context of all groups, allowing the critic to judge each group’s role beyond its local evidence. The process reward of each action is obtained by combining its action-level assessment with the refined group-level assessment of its group. We further use the generated process rewards to shape the GRPO Shao et al. (2024) advantage at each step, providing finer-grained credit assignment during policy optimization. We evaluate the framework on process-reward benchmarks and in downstream RL on OSWorld. The results show consistent improvements in process-reward accuracy and task success rate, demonstrating the effectiveness of adaptive-group process rewards. Our contributions are as follows: • We introduce an adaptive-group process reward framework for GUI agents, which dynamically partitions trajectories into semantically coherent subgoal groups to organize the evidence needed for process reward evaluation. • We design a two-level evaluation that assesses execution and contribution at both the action level and the group level, and obtain the process reward of each action by combining these assessments, making correct execution and group-level contribution jointly necessary. • Experiments on process reward benchmarks and downstream RL training demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. 2 Related Work 2.1 GUI Agents Recent progress in large language models and vision-language models has enabled GUI agents that interact with applications through visual observations and executable actions. Early systems mainly relied on prompting or supervised fine-tuning, while recent open-source models and frameworks, such as ShowUI Lin et al. (2024) , CogAgent Hong et al. (2024) , AGUVIS Xu et al. (2025) , UI-TARS Qin et al. (2025) , OpenCUA Wang et al. (2025) , Agent S Agashe et al. (2024) , and TongUI Zhang et al. (2025) , improve grounding, planning, and cross-platform interaction through larger GUI data and stronger vision-language-action modeling. More recently, reinforcement learning has become a central direction for GUI agents because it can optimize long-horizon interaction from environment feedback rather than only imitating fixed demonstrations. DART Li et al. (2025) decouples multi-turn rollout from training for GUI RL, UI-Genie Xiao et al. (2025) builds a reward-guided self-improvement loop for mobile GUI agents, Orcust Lu et al. (2025) combines principle-constrained reward modeling with online VM-grounded trajectory construction, and ClawGUI Tang et al. (2026) provides a full-stack infrastructure for GUI agent RL and deployment. However, most RL pipelines still rely heavily on sparse outcome rewards, which makes it difficult to assign credit to intermediate actions. Our work addresses this limitation by constructing dense process rewards over adaptive groups and the actions in those groups. 2.2 Process Reward Modeling Process reward modeling supplements sparse outcome rewards with feedback on intermediate steps, enabling more fine-grained credit assignment during training. In reasoning Lightman et al. (2023) ; Wang et al. (2023) and coding Le et al. (2022) ; Liu et al. (2023) ; Dai et al. (2026b) tasks, intermediate feedback can often be verified from execution results, compiler errors, unit tests, or other deterministic checks. GUI tasks provide no comparable automatic signal for most intermediate operations: the value of a click, text entry, menu selection, or file operation depends on visual state changes, task requirements, and subsequent operations. GUI process reward modeling must therefore infer both whether an action is correctly executed and its semantic role from trajectory context. Existing GUI process reward methods can be broadly organized into fixed-window step rewards Chen et al. (2025) ; Xiong et al. (2025) ; Xiao et al. (2025) ; Lu et al. (2025) ; Wan et al. (2026) and milestone rewards Zheng et al. (2026) ; Hao et al. (2026) ; Li et al. (2026a) ; Dai et al. (2026a) ; Zhai et al. (2026) . Fixed-window step rewards judge actions within a fixed local context. GUI-Shepherd Chen et al. (2025) learns step-level scores and rationales from human annotations, while GUI-PRA Xiong et al. (2025) selects historical context and actively perceives UI state changes to improve step-level judgment. SeekJudge Wan et al. (2026) further targets fine-grained step-level judgments for use within reinforcement learning. Milestone rewards organize feedback around predefined subgoals, checkpoints, or broader task-level structures. ADMIRE Zheng et al. (2026) dynamically distills verifiable milestones from successful explorations and applies asymmetric credit assignment to successful and failed trajectories. StainFlow Hao et al. (2026) tracks entity evidence to derive task stages and links relevant steps for key-node verification, while GUIDE Zhai et al. (2026) decomposes completed trajectories into subtask units for structured diagnosis. These approaches organize action judgment within preset local contexts or task-level structures, whereas our adaptive-group framework dynamically partitions the executed trajectory into semantically coherent subgoal groups and combines execution and contribution at both the action level and the group level to assign each action a process reward. 3 Method 3.1 Problem Formulation We formulate solving a GUI task as a sequential interaction between an agent and an environment. Given a task instruction g g , the agent observes the GUI state o t o_{t} at each step. Conditioned on this observation and the interaction history, it generates a response c t c_{t} with an executable action a t a_{t} . Executing a t a_{t} changes the environment and produces the next observation o t + 1 o_{t+1} . An executed trajectory is therefore represented as τ = ( o 0 , c 0 , a 0 , o 1 , c 1 , a 1 , … , o T − 1 , c T − 1 , a T − 1 , o T ) , \tau=(o_{0},c_{0},a_{0},o_{1},c_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{T-1},c_{T-1},a_{T-1},o_{T}), (1) where T T is the number of executed actions. The response c t c_{t} provides the agent’s textual intent, while the observations and executed actions record the interaction with GUI. After the trajectory is completed, the environment or a task verifier V V produces an outcome reward R = V ⁡ ( g , τ ) R=V(g,\tau) . This trajectory-level signal does not directly indicate the value of individual actions. We therefore formulate GUI process reward generation as producing a process reward for every executed action: ( r 0 pr , r 1 pr , … , r T − 1 pr ) = ϕ ⁡ ( g , τ ) , (r_{0}^{\mathrm{pr}},r_{1}^{\mathrm{pr}},\ldots,r_{T-1}^{\mathrm{pr}})=\phi(g,\tau), (2) where ϕ \phi is a process reward model and r t pr r_{t}^{\mathrm{pr}} is the process reward of action a t a_{t} at step t t . As shown in figure 2 , we instantiate ϕ \phi by first partitioning τ \tau into adaptive groups that define the context for judging each action (section 3.2 ), then generating action-level and group-level assessments (section 3.3 ). The resulting process rewards are used to shape GRPO’s step-level advantage during policy optimization (section 3.4 ). Figure 2: Overview of the proposed framework. (a) A grouping critic partitions the trajectory from the instruction and responses into subgoal groups. (b) Two-level scoring produces an action-level score and a refined group-level score, which are used to generate the process rewards. (c) The process rewards shape the GRPO advantage. 3.2 Adaptive-Group Trajectory Partitioning Fixed-window step rewards evaluate an action within a preset local context, while milestone rewards organize credit around predefined checkpoints. Neither evidence scope is determined by the trajectory that was actually executed. We recover subgoals from the executed trajectory instead. Grouping should follow executed intents, which are already stated in each c t c_{t} , so we use a grouping critic F part F_{\mathrm{part}} to partition the trajectory from the instruction g g and the responses { c t } t = 0 T − 1 \{c_{t}\}_{t=0}^{T-1} : { G k } k = 1 K = F part ​ ( g , { c t } t = 0 T − 1 ) , G k = ( n k , ℐ k ) . \{G_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}=F_{\mathrm{part}}(g,\{c_{t}\}_{t=0}^{T-1}),\qquad G_{k}=(n_{k},\mathcal{I}_{k}). (3) The result is a contiguous, non-overlapping partition of the trajectory: each G k G_{k} consists of a hypothesized subgoal n k n_{k} and the step indices ℐ k \mathcal{I}_{k} of the group, and k ⁡ ( t ) k(t) denotes the unique group of step t t . The subgoal n k n_{k} is not a required milestone of g g , so valid executions can induce different groups. These groups are the context for the judgments below. 3.3 Adaptive-Group Process Reward Generation The adaptive group defines the context for judging its actions and supports two complementary levels of evaluation: how an action contributes to the group’s subgoal, and how the subgoal contributes to the overall task. At the action level, the critic assesses whether each action is correctly executed and whether it advances the group’s subgoal. At the group level, it aggregates these assessments to judge the group’s subgoal completion and contribution to the global task, then revisits the group-level assessments using all groups as context. We evaluate the proposed process rewards on two process-reward benchmarks and for reinforcement learning on OSWorld applications. CUARewardBench Lin et al. (2026) is built on OSWorld trajectories from 10 desktop software categories and 7 agents; it annotates key good and bad actions, and we report process-reward results compared to the benchmark’s OpenCUA-Reflector Wang et al. (2025) and SE-WSM Sun et al. (2025) prompt templates. CUAStepBench Wan et al. (2026) densely annotates every step on executed computer-use trajectories and pairs these labels with human trajectory-level verdicts, covering 177 applications across platforms. OSWorld Xie et al. (2025) provides open-ended GUI tasks in a real desktop environment, with success judged by execution-based scripts on the final state; we train and test on its Chrome, LibreOffice Impress, and LibreOffice Calc applications. Metrics. CUARewardBench treats each step judgment as a binary decision against a human label. We use a threshold of 0.4 0.4 to separate positive and negative predictions. We follow the benchmark protocol: precision (P) and negative predictive value (NPV) measure how reliable a positive or negative verdict is, while recall (R), specificity (S), and overall accuracy (OA) summarize coverage and overall correctness. On CUAStepBench, every step carries a binary human label, and we score the predicted step judgments by precision (P), recall (R), and F1. OSWorld success is determined by execution-based scripts on the final desktop state; we report both a single-run success rate and the mean over three runs. Implementation. We use Qwen3.6-27B Qwen Team (2026) for F part F_{\mathrm{part}} , F ref F_{\mathrm{ref}} , F act F_{\mathrm{act}} , F grp F_{\mathrm{grp}} , and F rev F_{\mathrm{rev}} . We build on the open-source DART-GUI infrastructure Li et al. (2025) for reinforcement learning: multi-turn OSWorld rollouts are collected independently of training, stored, and consumed by an asynchronous GRPO trainer. Our framework for process-reward generation is integrated as an additional asynchronous stage on completed trajectories, and the trainer then uses these process rewards to shape the GRPO advantage of the base model UI-TARS-1.5-7B Qin et al. (2025) . Rollouts use N = 8 N=8 trajectories per instruction, 15 concurrent environments, a maximum of 30 environment steps, and sampling temperature 0.7 0.7 ; each action is generated with at most 5 images and 35 text turns of history.
